the-drug-war-without-cops.supporting_excerpt: Bloomberg's war on smoking showed that it is possible for a society to have a meaningful impact on the level of consumption of a harmful, addictive substance through tools other than policing and incarceration. ... Policymakers have many options between incarceration and commercialization. More specifically, nonenforcement tools for vice suppression, like the ones Bloomberg used to such effect, deserve more attention. Approaches like low-enforcement prohibition, prevention programming, public health campaigns and public disapproval of substance use have a lot of power — if we accept that they have a place in the drug-control arsenal.

But unlike the police, not everyone is plugged into a system of emergency response that can get them to the scene of an overdose in minutes, when minutes count. We have a responsibility to shrink the number of Black and brown families unnecessarily caught in the child protective system. Two of Spinak's primary calls for change are inarguable: We need to limit the number of calls to the child abuse/neglect hotline, which can be a tool not only for state abuse but for intrafamily abuse as well. This should lead policymakers to embracing a range of proven hyperlocal interventions that are genuinely responsive to crime complaints of people in neighborhoods, so that we not only have a good chance of driving crime down but at the same time build public confidence that we're being responsive to specific conditions. Life inside is intended to be "normal," with incarcerated people living in units where they cook together, in facilities where they are trained and connected to work upon release. ... There are examples to draw from in Pennsylvania, this model is being used in a portion of the prison system, called Little Scandinavia. There are examples to draw from in Montgomery County, Maryland, Travis County, Texas, among other places. Why can't New York aspire to a similar ideal?

new-york-needs-more-than-3300-jail-beds.title: New York Needs More Than 3,300 Jail Beds
new-york-needs-more-than-3300-jail-beds.policy_ask: New York City should increase the planned borough jail capacity beyond 3,300 beds to safely accommodate the pretrial detention population.
new-york-needs-more-than-3300-jail-beds.rationale: The article clearly expresses a policy preference (capacity must increase) but does not explicitly recommend a specific action to a named government actor or agency.
new-york-needs-more-than-3300-jail-beds.supporting_excerpt: 3,300 beds is simply not enough space to safely detain all of the people New York needs to hold each day. ... At almost no point in the six years between 2016 and 2022 could the Rikers population have plausibly been reduced by category such that it was below 3,300. ... Safe, humane and effective jails are essential for the nation's biggest city to have. But jails aren't safe and humane if they're overcrowded, and they aren't effective if violent criminals aren't detained for lack of space.

jimmy-breslin-and-the-lost-rhythm-of-new.rationale: This is a nostalgic essay and book review about Jimmy Breslin's legacy as a newspaper columnist; it analyzes and laments the decline of the form but makes no specific policy recommendation directed at any government actor.

fixing-the-research-to-policy-pipeline.title: Fixing the Research-to-Policy Pipeline
fixing-the-research-to-policy-pipeline.policy_ask: Research funders and academic institutions should require pre-registration of all randomized controlled trials to improve the credibility of evidence-based policy.
fixing-the-research-to-policy-pipeline.target: Research funders and academic organizations (named examples: Arnold Ventures, American Economic Association)
fixing-the-research-to-policy-pipeline.rationale: The article articulates a clear policy preference (pre-registration as a solution) but frames it mostly analytically, discussing existing practices rather than explicitly recommending specific actors adopt or expand the practice.
fixing-the-research-to-policy-pipeline.supporting_excerpt: The primary way to address this challenge is one that is now quite widespread: pre-registration of all RCTs conducted. Pre-registration means that researchers create a public record that a study is planned, as well as some basic information about it. Many research funders (including Arnold Ventures) now require this, as does the American Economic Association (if you want the option to publish your study in one of its prestigious journals). This ensures we have a record of all studies that were conducted, before they got underway.

when-cant-miss-programs-fail.title: When ‘Can’t Miss’ Programs Fail
when-cant-miss-programs-fail.policy_ask: Government and philanthropy should fund more experimentation, evaluation, and iteration of social programs, and avoid immediately cutting resources from programs with null results.
when-cant-miss-programs-fail.rationale: Clear policy preference is articulated (fund experimentation, don't defund failed programs, conduct more RCTs), but no specific named agency or official is directed to act.
when-cant-miss-programs-fail.supporting_excerpt: We need a lot more experimentation, a lot more evaluation and a lot more iteration. Discovering scalable solutions to social problems is highly valuable. So even if it takes 50 tries to discover an effective intervention, it can be worth it. Since the benefits of solving social problems can rarely be monetized by the innovators, government and philanthropy need to be more generous and more strategic in funding experimentation. For example, rather than immediately cutting off resources from programs that produce a null evaluation result, funders should consider reinvesting in them so that program leaders can use the evaluation findings to improve their service delivery models.

its-hard-to-change-people.title: It’s Hard to Change People
its-hard-to-change-people.rationale: This is analytical and philosophical—examining why crime policy interventions fail—but takes no concrete policy position or recommendation directed at any government actor.

raising-the-bar-and-ending-an-era-of-low.rationale: The piece is largely analytical and philosophical about government decision-making and evidence gaps, with implicit normative views (better research, focus on system rules) but no specific recommendation directed at a named actor.

democracy-of-evidence.title: Democracy of Evidence
democracy-of-evidence.policy_ask: Government agencies and nonprofits should conduct their own internal econometric evaluations of policy outcomes rather than relying exclusively on external academic evaluators.
democracy-of-evidence.rationale: The article articulates a clear policy preference (democratize econometric tools, shift evaluation work from academics to practitioners) but does not name a specific agency or official to implement this change, and no concrete actionable steps are prescribed.
democracy-of-evidence.supporting_excerpt: Government offices, nonprofit organizations and other agents of social change make specific policies for specific populations, and they do so on a daily basis, yet they rarely measure whether their policies have the intended effects. More often, they rely on intuition or politics to guide their decisions. When they do conduct evaluations, they are cumbersome affairs involving protracted timelines and external evaluators, usually from academia. This is an unnecessary process, particularly applied to the workaday policies that directly affect most people's lives. ... The solution is not to abandon the economic tools that make causal research possible, but instead to put them in more hands and apply them to smaller problems — a democratization of knowledge generation that could itself be a big social change.

causal-research-more-not-less.title: Causal Research: More, Not Less
causal-research-more-not-less.rationale: The article advocates for more causal research and better research practices (publishing null results, replication before scaling) but makes no specific actionable recommendation directed at a named government actor or agency.

new-york-needs-remedial-education-in-civ.title: New York Needs Remedial Education in Civic Tech
new-york-needs-remedial-education-in-civ.policy_ask: The City should redirect MyCity funding toward hiring internal tech talent and fixing critical Department of Education systems rather than pursuing the portal project.
new-york-needs-remedial-education-in-civ.target: Mayor Adams / City of New York (implicit)
new-york-needs-remedial-education-in-civ.rationale: The article clearly expresses a policy preference (abandon MyCity, prioritize DOE systems, hire internal talent) but stops short of a direct, named recommendation to a specific actor with concrete next steps.
new-york-needs-remedial-education-in-civ.supporting_excerpt: Not only does Adams' plan trap the city's few technical resources in a technical fantasy land, it detracts from solving the most pressing technical problems for New Yorkers. ... Instead of throwing money in the circular file, rinse and repeat, the City could use the same money to hire internal tech talent.

saved-by-the-camera.title: Saved By the Camera
saved-by-the-camera.policy_ask: New York City should use red-light and speed-camera data to prevent vehicles with five or more traffic violations from operating on city roads.
saved-by-the-camera.target: New York City (unspecified agency, likely NYPD or DOT)
saved-by-the-camera.rationale: The article makes a specific, actionable policy recommendation with clear criteria (vehicles with 5+ tickets) and a named jurisdiction, but does not specify which city agency should execute it.
saved-by-the-camera.supporting_excerpt: If New York City had been able to keep vehicles with five or more speed- or red-light tickets off the roads in 2022, the city could have saved as many as 26 lives, out of the total of 142 lives lost in this 2022 dataset, reducing the death toll by 18%. With enabling state legislation, the city should use camera data to take vehicles (exempting emergency vehicles like ambulances) with five or more speed or red-light tickets within one year off the road.

can-new-york-become-a-city-of-yes.title: Can New York Become a City of Yes?
can-new-york-become-a-city-of-yes.policy_ask: The Adams administration should implement zoning reforms and incentives to enable development of underutilized land and accessory dwelling units to increase housing supply.
can-new-york-become-a-city-of-yes.target: Mayor Eric Adams / City of New York government
can-new-york-become-a-city-of-yes.rationale: Clear preference for pro-housing policies and specific ideas (zoning reform, ADUs, vacant lot development) but no concrete action steps or formal recommendation directed at a named official or agency.
can-new-york-become-a-city-of-yes.supporting_excerpt: New York — yes, even this most dense of American cities — has a vast trove of underutilized land. Outside of Manhattan, 92% of buildings within one kilometer (0.62 miles) of a subway stop are three stories or less. The city has 10 square miles of vacant lots zoned for residential use. If developed at the same density as the Park Slope neighborhood in Brooklyn (Community District 6), this land could yield at least 340,000 units. Furthermore, the Big Apple has over half a million one- and two-family homes. As a thought experiment, if each added an accessory dwelling unit — a "granny flat" or converted garage — or created a new unit through subdivision, the Adams administration could achieve its objective without displacing a single tenant.

understanding-the-new-york-news-subsidy.title: Extra, Extra: Understanding the New York News Subsidy
understanding-the-new-york-news-subsidy.rationale: The article analyzes New York's news subsidy law and identifies regulatory gaps, but stops short of recommending specific actions that Empire State Development or other actors should take.

when-zoning-goes-too-far.title: When Zoning Goes Too Far
when-zoning-goes-too-far.policy_ask: NYC policymakers should modernize and significantly relax the zoning code to permit the mixed-use, mixed-density neighborhoods that historically defined the city.
when-zoning-goes-too-far.rationale: Clear policy preference (zoning restrictions are too tight and should be loosened) but no specific action, timeline, or named agency is directed to act.
when-zoning-goes-too-far.supporting_excerpt: Over the past 60 years, even as we have gained a greater appreciation for New York's historic character, New York City policymakers have implemented increasingly complicated regulations that — intentionally or not — have banned the very things that define our city's character. ... Even in 1961, it did not match the actual way that New Yorkers lived and worked: Commercial strips with ground-floor offices, restaurants or services like laundromats or grocery stores that were built prior to the 1960s exist across the five boroughs, but in many cases were banned moving forward by the use restrictions, height and density limits, or parking requirements created in the 1961 zoning resolution. ... It's time for an update.

new-yorks-new-housing-deal-a-significant.title: New York’s New Housing Deal: A Significant Win for Tenants
new-yorks-new-housing-deal-a-significant.rationale: Article analyzes and evaluates an already-enacted housing budget deal; it does not recommend any new action by a government actor.

smarter-parking-policy-please.title: Smarter Parking Policy, Please
smarter-parking-policy-please.policy_ask: City Hall should reallocate street space from parking to bike lanes, bus lanes, and wider sidewalks, leveraging the congestion pricing opportunity.
smarter-parking-policy-please.rationale: Clear policy preference for reallocating curb space away from cars, but no specific named city agency or official is directed to act.
smarter-parking-policy-please.supporting_excerpt: The road to a city that's less dependent on cars runs through the curb lane. That is where New York must build far more world-class bike and bus lanes, fixing and expanding a network that is incomplete and hampered by illegally parked cars and turning drivers. This is also where, in the pre-automobile days, wider sidewalks once gave New Yorkers ample room to walk. The city doesn't necessarily need to zap parking spaces, as opposed to moving lanes, to make these changes. But at a bare minimum, it needs to move them.

build-better-for-bicyclists.title: Build Better for Bicyclists
build-better-for-bicyclists.policy_ask: The City should improve streets for bicyclists, particularly by expanding protected bike lanes running east-west across Manhattan.
build-better-for-bicyclists.target: New York City (unnamed specific agency, though implicitly Department of Transportation)
build-better-for-bicyclists.rationale: The article makes a clear, specific policy preference (better bike infrastructure and protected lanes) directed at the city government, but does not name the specific agency or official responsible for implementation.
build-better-for-bicyclists.supporting_excerpt: There are few protected bike lanes running east-west in Manhattan, and those demarcated with a few white stripes are ignored more than yellow lights. ... Once traffic is reduced, we need to immediately reclaim asphalt for dedicated bus and bike lanes, which must be fully protected by islands that separate bikers from traffic.

serve-the-walkers.title: Serve the Walkers
serve-the-walkers.policy_ask: The State should grant the City power to reduce default speed limits to 20 mph, expand red-light and speed camera limits citywide, and allow speed cameras outside school zones; the City should then deploy cameras on high-injury two-way streets.
serve-the-walkers.target: New York State (Governor Hochul and lawmakers) and New York City government
serve-the-walkers.rationale: Specific, actionable recommendations directed at named state and city actors, but the city's role is somewhat secondary (contingent on state action first).
serve-the-walkers.supporting_excerpt: The State should similarly give the City the power to increase the number of red-light and speed cameras, currently limited citywide to 150 intersections and 750 zones within a quarter-mile of a school respectively. Third, within Manhattan, the State should allow speed cameras outside of school zones, to which current law confines them. Once it has secured expanded state authorization for camera enforcement, the City should target two-way streets, such as Canal Street, 23rd Street and 57th Street ... such streets, according to one city report, account for a disproportionate number of injuries and deaths relative to their percentage of the street network.

offer-riders-a-better-deal.title: Offer Riders a Better Deal
offer-riders-a-better-deal.policy_ask: Lower subway, bus, and commuter rail fares by 10% on the day congestion pricing begins, funded by half of the expected $1 billion in congestion pricing revenue.
offer-riders-a-better-deal.rationale: Specific, actionable recommendation with clear dollar amount and timing, but the broader government actor (the city or state) that would need to authorize this isn't explicitly named as the decision-maker.
offer-riders-a-better-deal.supporting_excerpt: A simple solution would be to lower the subway, bus and commuter rail fares on the same day the congestion pricing charge begins. If approximately half of the expected $1 billion in revenue from the congestion charge were used to reduce fares, the city could announce an unprecedented 10% reduction in all subway and bus fares, and a commitment to not increase them for the foreseeable future.

the-long-and-winding-road.title: The Long and Winding Road
the-long-and-winding-road.rationale: This is a historical narrative and explainer tracing congestion pricing's political trajectory from 1977 to 2019; it analyzes the politics but makes no forward-looking policy recommendation or call to action.

risks-outside-the-zone.title: Risks Outside the Zone
risks-outside-the-zone.policy_ask: Transit officials and legislators must allocate congestion pricing revenue to prioritize service improvements (signal modernization, frequency increases, expansions) in the Bronx and Northern Manhattan rather than only maintenance upgrades.
risks-outside-the-zone.rationale: Clear policy preference stated (revenue allocation toward service improvements in underserved areas), but no specific action steps, timeline, or concrete dollar amounts requested.
risks-outside-the-zone.supporting_excerpt: But the only projects for the Bronx are ADA upgrades, depot and rail yard upgrades, fan and power facility upgrades, and some structural repairs on the 6 train — no signal modernization, frequency improvements or expansions. ... Improving air quality in the Bronx means getting cars off the road, which necessitates getting people onto public transit. ... Alleviating this will require using congestion pricing revenue to bolster bus frequency, something the state Legislature started to address by committing $12 million to more buses in the city.

invest-in-transit-the-right-way.title: Invest in Transit the Right Way
invest-in-transit-the-right-way.policy_ask: The MTA should use congestion pricing revenues to fund visible improvements in capital spending (new lines, faster service, station accessibility) and operations (bus modernization, increased service frequency), while prioritizing cost-efficient designs and operational improvements over expansive new construction.
invest-in-transit-the-right-way.rationale: Clear, specific recommendations directed at the MTA regarding how to spend congestion pricing revenue, though the article frames this as guidance/strategy rather than a formal mandate from government.
invest-in-transit-the-right-way.supporting_excerpt: On the capital side, this means the agency must continue to find cost savings through more efficient designs and spend the money on visible improvements, including new lines, faster service and station accessibility. On the operations side, improvements can use the expected speed boost from reduced congestion to build up a bus modernization program; the most pressing improvements do not require more spending, but do require managers to be more willing to expand service and let higher ridership pay for it. ... The most important lesson from this is that the MTA will be judged based on its ability to deliver projects that make a difference to those who use the system regardless of the extra money.

congestion-pricing-an-explainer.title: Congestion Pricing: An Explainer
congestion-pricing-an-explainer.rationale: This is a straightforward explainer article on congestion pricing's history, mechanics, and public opinion—pure analysis with no policy recommendation directed at any government actor.

business-fears-real-and-imagined.title: Business Fears, Real and Imagined
business-fears-real-and-imagined.rationale: The article presents congestion pricing as already implemented policy, documents business opposition, and raises analytical questions about economic effects, but makes no specific recommendation to any government actor about what should be done.

beware-of-potholes.policy_ask: The MTA should implement stronger enforcement mechanisms to prevent license plate fraud and gaming of the congestion pricing system.
beware-of-potholes.rationale: The article expresses clear concern about gaps in congestion pricing enforcement and identifies specific problems (plate fraud, defacement), but stops short of prescribing concrete actions the MTA should take.
beware-of-potholes.supporting_excerpt: Here's a rundown of the shenanigans, all of which are illegal and many of which, under legislation passed last week, can result in fines of up to $500. ... New Yorkers have imaginatively figured out a plethora of means to thwart the license plate readers, even before congestion pricing. ... Transit enforcers need to keep an eye out for too-clever-by-half workarounds.

willets-point-and-the-making-of-a-neighb.title: Willets Point and the Making of a Neighborhood
willets-point-and-the-making-of-a-neighb.rationale: This is primarily analytical and descriptive—examining the Willets Point development project, its affordability claims, and neighborhood context—without pivoting to a specific policy recommendation or action request.

bring-vision-to-hochuls-mental-health-pl.title: Bring Vision to Hochul’s Mental Health Plans
bring-vision-to-hochuls-mental-health-pl.policy_ask: Governor Hochul should develop and articulate a comprehensive, strategized mental health transformation plan that specifies target psychiatric bed numbers, their distribution across facility types, and how they integrate with community-based programs.
bring-vision-to-hochuls-mental-health-pl.target: Governor Kathy Hochul / New York State Office of Mental Health
bring-vision-to-hochuls-mental-health-pl.rationale: The article clearly expresses a policy preference (Hochul needs a more coherent mental health strategy with explicit goals), but stops short of requesting a specific concrete action or measurable target.
bring-vision-to-hochuls-mental-health-pl.supporting_excerpt: [closest]: But what, exactly, Hochul is trying to "transform," and into what, begs clarification so that all the people and institutions involved in the complex mental health system understand where New York intends to head and why. ... How many beds New York needs is an important and complex question that has to do with who the population is, where they live and what kind of care — short-term or long-term — they require. ... But the critics are on to something when they characterize Hochul's moves as reactive, not guided by long-term strategic vision.

the-congestion-pricing-meltdown-and-its-.supporting_excerpt: When New York Gov. Among many other urgent capital priorities, congestion pricing was slated to modernize the clunky signal system from the 1930s, allowing faster, more frequent service less prone to breakdowns. The program was going to raise billions for elevators, affording New Yorkers who can't climb stairs access to many more destinations, far more quickly than the bus or Access-A-Ride paratransit system allows. And while dedicated to infrastructure upgrades, the toll would also take fiscal pressure off day-to-day operations, reducing the likelihood of longer waits due to service cuts.

Under state law, elected officials and state employees are barred from accepting gifts above $75 from an "interested source," or someone who does business with the state or hopes to in the future and wants to affect decisions. ... City laws and rules are even more permissive when it comes to travel expenses. This strategy needs enforcement that is consistent, sustained and focused on the right targets, all as part of a broader collaboration with the community. ... Between 74th and 111th Streets, robberies have surged 44% from last year and 141% since 2019, while assaults are up 46% and 118% respectively during those periods. a-rare-remedy-to-the-persistent-brutalit.supporting_excerpt: The broad powers and the independence of the position offer the last, best option to fix an entrenched problem of long duration. But unlike an executive appointee, the receiver retains its independence because it is appointed by and reports only to the court. the-missing-fingerprints-at-crime-scenes.supporting_excerpt: Against this backdrop, policymakers who believe there's a need for stronger gun safety rules in America should look for new ways to impose and enforce regulations on gun manufacturers, distributors, marketers and dealers. Industry regulation — not just controlling the behavior of individual consumers — is a critical tool in policymaking that has curbed other public health crises. For example, in addition to licensing drivers, we force car companies to make cars safer. We both set age minimums for cigarette purchases and prohibit tobacco companies from marketing to kids. In addition to criminalizing the possession of narcotics, we limit prescription opioid production. States can take inspiration from these approaches when it comes to combating gun violence within their borders.

the-80-20-rule-of-gun-supply.rationale: Clear policy preference and direction (supply-side focus on problem dealers) but no specific named agency or concrete action is requested; 'we should start by focusing' expresses intent without directing anyone to do anything specific.
the-80-20-rule-of-gun-supply.supporting_excerpt: While the majority of licensed gun dealers in the U.S. operate legally, a small fraction are responsible for feeding the lion's share of the illegal supply. One estimate suggests that just 5% of dealers are linked to nearly 90% of crime guns recovered by law enforcement. If we want to curb gun violence using a supply-side strategy, we should start by focusing on the small group of dealers doing the most harm. Sure, we could pour resources into endlessly repairing the leaks that spring throughout the system — but doesn't it make more sense to fix the faucets?

before-the-trigger-is-pulled.title: Before the Trigger Is Pulled

before-the-trigger-is-pulled.rationale: The author identifies a clear policy preference (reorienting deterrence strategy toward gun-carrying) but does not name a specific government actor or agency responsible for implementing this change.
before-the-trigger-is-pulled.supporting_excerpt: The overwhelming cause of gun violence is arguments that end in impulse shootings — meaning, the shooter didn't set out to fire his weapon and might not even have "meant to" until he was overcome by the urge to do so in the heat of a moment. This finding leads to an important policy insight. Deterrence might have more of an impact if it is focused on the behavior that is the precursor (and necessary condition) of most shootings in America: illegal gun-carrying itself. And contrary to the in-the-moment, passion-driven decision to swing a fist or pull a trigger, the decision to take a gun with them on their way to the party or the mall is more likely to be rational and deliberate — and hence deterrable.

building-better-piece-by-piece.supporting_excerpt: In the United States, approximately 4% of new construction is manufactured off-site — mostly single-story buildings. the-property-tax-cannot-stand.supporting_excerpt: Assessment caps for small homeowners (Class 1) limit assessment increases to 6% per year and 20% over five years. This, along with the City's failure to adopt a uniform assessment ratio (assessment divided by market value) within Class 1, means that in neighborhoods with fast-rising property values, assessments are kept low, resulting in lower tax bills than would have otherwise been the case. ... In multifamily buildings, rentals pay a disproportionate share of the property tax levy compared to very expensive cooperatives and condominiums. ... Co-ops and condos, regardless of how fancy they are, are valued by comparing them to rental income from regulated, rather than from market-rate, rental buildings. new-yorks-next-mayor-must-put-heads-toge.supporting_excerpt: This year marks the 50th anniversary of one of the city's finest moments of civic cooperation: the Municipal Assistance Corporation (MAC), the public-private partnership that rescued New York from bankruptcy. In 1975, when the federal government largely refused to help, Gov. Hugh Carey looked to an unlikely coalition of bankers, union heads and local leaders to negotiate New York's survival. The spirit of '75 was about more than horse trading or financial engineering; it was a feat of civic imagination, rooted in the conviction that seemingly disparate interests — public and private, city and state — must work together towards a better future. 50 years later, New York needs that spirit — one guided by give and take, pragmatism over pieties and shared resolve in the face of shared challenges — again.

Teams go door to door, speak directly with residents, and then carry out a coordinated set of actions within a concentrated area over the course of a week: repairing sidewalks, boarding vacant properties, clearing lots, removing trash and connecting residents to social services. ... Pairing cleanup operations with structured door-to-door outreach, modeled on Buffalo's Clean Sweep, could make city presence more visible and meaningful in historically underserved neighborhoods. ... rubber-meets-road-lighting-policy-detail.supporting_excerpt: Better lighting on a city's streets and sidewalks can be a highly effective way to reduce crime — and to bolster civic life at the same time. In New York City, a randomized controlled trial in public housing showed a 35% reduction in major crime committed outdoors during nighttime hours, with no increase in nearby areas. This guide for policymakers explains why improving lighting makes cities safer and summarizes the research supporting streetlights as an effective crime prevention strategy. It also outlines important considerations and practical steps for implementing a simple change that yields outsize benefits.

rubber-meets-road-lighting-summary.supporting_excerpt: In New York City, researchers identified 80 public housing developments with high crime rates and installed temporary lights in half of them. The new lights reduced outdoor nighttime index crimes by 35%, and the drop in crime occurred without any increase in arrests. In Philadelphia, upgrading more than 34,000 streetlights in high-crime neighborhoods to provide brighter and more even light reduced nighttime outdoor crimes by 15% in comparison to neighborhoods where there were no changes in lighting, including a 20% drop in violent crimes and 21% reduction in gun crimes. Improved street lighting is easy to implement through existing municipal operations, and it yields immediate results. In New York City, for example, it costs $10,000 to install a single new streetlight (a capital expense if the project exceeds $50,000 within a half-mile radius). This is a fraction of the cost of crime and punishment, and far less expensive than employing additional police officers.

These easy-to-deploy curb-adjacent and parking-adjacent bus lanes, however, haven't been paired with other changes to convey substantive priority by addressing conflicts with other vehicles that delay buses, notably at intersections. The Atlas illustrates how an extensive set of tools can be combined into broader priority strategies that rearrange the hierarchy of streets and shape circulation patterns, for example, by diverting through traffic away from transit routes or by establishing priority corridors for transit. ... These localized interventions, when embedded in broader traffic management strategies that favor transit by systematically addressing the sources of delays, have delivered faster, more reliable, and cheaper-to-operate trams and buses in cities like Zürich, Munich, Prague, Lyon, Stockholm and many more examples detailed in the Atlas.
